templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, whose stated mission is to give {client.plural} service they can rely on. At the end of a busy day you could skip the last step of {task|the}. Nobody checks it, and skipping it would let you leave ten minutes early.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Do the last step, because your small part helps the workplace keep its promise to {client.plural}.
options.why: Routine steps are part of how a workplace delivers on its mission. Your work connects to what {client.plural} experience, even when no one is watching.

options.text: Skip it, since a step that nobody checks cannot affect what {client.plural} will receive in the end.
options.why: A step that is not checked still exists for a reason. Skipping it removes a safeguard that {client.plural} may be depending on.
options.misconception: If nobody checks it, it does not matter.

options.text: Skip it today and make up for it by doing the step twice as carefully tomorrow instead.
options.why: Tomorrow's extra care cannot cover today's gap. The work done today is what {client.plural} experience today.
options.misconception: I can make up for a skipped step later.

options.text: Do the step only if someone in charge happens to walk by, since that is when it counts.
options.why: Doing the work only when watched treats it as a show instead of a responsibility. The mission is served when the work is done every time.
options.misconception: Work only matters when someone sees it.

templates.principle: Connect routine tasks to the workplace's mission: small steps help deliver what the organization promises, whether or not anyone checks.

review.notes: Mission is stated in the scenario; no policy dependence.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You notice an error in {document|a} prepared by another department. Your workplace asks employees to report concerns about other departments to their own {lead}, who then contacts that department.

options.text: Tell your own {lead} about the error, so the concern reaches the other department through the usual route.
options.why: Following the reporting structure makes sure the right people hear about the problem in an organized way, and your {lead} may know context you do not.

options.text: Fix the error yourself in {document|a} and send it back, so the other department does not have to be bothered.
options.why: Changing another department's work without telling them can create confusion and hides the problem that caused it.
options.misconception: Fixing it myself is faster than reporting it.

options.text: Email the other department's manager directly, since that person has the most authority over the error.
options.why: Going around your own {lead} skips the route your workplace set up and may surprise people who need to know first.
options.misconception: The highest-ranking person is always the best one to contact.

options.text: Mention it to a coworker and hope that someone who knows what to do will take care of it.
options.why: A casual comment does not guarantee the information reaches anyone who can act on it. Reports work best when they go through a defined route.

templates.principle: Know how your organization is structured and use its channels: report concerns about other departments through your own lead.

review.notes: Reporting structure is stated in the scenario.

templates.timing: The reporting structure sets the first step; the sequence matters.

templates.scenario: At {workplace|the}, your team routinely prints full-color paper copies of {document|a} that are read once and thrown away. You notice that this costs money and creates a lot of waste, and a digital copy would work just as well.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Suggest to your {lead} a digital option, and explain the savings and the waste it would avoid.
options.why: A clear proposal that covers both cost and environmental effect gives the decision-maker what they need, and it improves the workplace beyond your own tasks.

options.text: Keep printing the copies the same way, since the cost of supplies is the company's concern, not yours.
options.why: Everyone's habits add up to the workplace's costs and waste. A good idea is worth sharing with the person who can approve it.
options.misconception: Costs are only the owner's concern.

options.text: Stop printing the copies on your own and send only digital versions, without telling anyone why.
options.why: Changing a team practice alone can leave people without something they expect. A proposal lets the team decide together.
options.misconception: I should act on a good idea without asking.

options.text: Ask coworkers to print less on their own, and hope that the habit spreads across the team over time.
options.why: Informal requests rarely change a team's routine, and they leave out the person who can actually change it.
options.misconception: Quiet encouragement is enough to change a process.

templates.principle: Consider cost and environmental effects of routine habits, and bring better options to the person who can approve a change.

templates.prompt: Tap the line that conflicts with the workplace's mission.

segments.text: Our mission is to provide safe, dependable service to our community.
segments.whyFine: A statement of the mission, stated plainly.

segments.text: To save time this month, we will skip the final quality and safety check.
segments.why: Skipping the final check contradicts the stated mission of safe, dependable service.

segments.text: We will keep our prices where they are for now.
segments.whyFine: Keeping prices steady does not conflict with the mission.

segments.text: I would like your feedback before Friday.
segments.whyFine: Asking for feedback is a normal part of a plan.

templates.principle: Check plans against the organization's mission: shortcuts that undercut what the workplace promises are a problem.

review.notes: Only one line contradicts the stated mission.

templates.scenario: You want to suggest a change to how a routine task is done at {workplace|the}.
templates.prompt: Put these steps in a sensible order.

steps.text: Learn how the task supports the workplace's goals
Identify who would be affected by a change
Weigh the costs and effects, including on the environment

precedence.why: You need to know what the task is for before you can tell who it touches.
Knowing who is affected helps you weigh the effects fully.
A suggestion is stronger when you have already weighed its effects.

templates.principle: Propose changes responsibly: understand the goal, see who is affected, weigh the effects, then present your idea.

templates.scenario: Your {lead} at {workplace|the} asks for your input on choosing between two suppliers. Supplier A is cheaper but ships from far away in heavy single-use packaging. Supplier B costs slightly more, is local, and uses reusable packaging. Your {lead} has mentioned that cost matters.

options.text: Lay out cost, delivery and packaging effects for both, and recommend one with your reasoning.
options.why: Cost matters, but so do the effects on the environment and community. Presenting the full picture helps your {lead} decide with all the facts.

options.text: Recommend Supplier A, since your {lead} said cost matters and it is clearly the cheaper one.
options.why: Cost is a real factor, but recommending on price alone leaves out the packaging and shipping effects that your {lead} would also want to weigh.
options.misconception: The factor mentioned first is the only one that counts.

options.text: Recommend Supplier B, since local and reusable options are always better no matter what they cost.
options.why: Environmental benefits are important, but ignoring a cost difference leaves out something the workplace has to consider.
options.misconception: Environmental benefits outweigh every other factor.

options.text: Tell your {lead} you have no opinion, since choosing a supplier is not something you decide.
options.why: You were asked for input. Sharing what you can see helps even when someone else makes the decision.
options.misconception: If I do not make the decision, I should stay out of it.

templates.principle: Weigh cost together with effects on the community and environment, and present the full picture when asked for input.
